newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish PM refuses comment on CIA Rushdie report.
newsitem.headline: Danish PM refuses comment on CIA Rushdie report.

text.p: Danish Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen declined on Monday to comment on media reports that the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) had warned him of a possible attempt to kill British author Salman Rushdie during a visit to Copenhagen last month.

"I have nothing new to add on this question. I had a clear basis for the decisions I took along with my colleagues in the government. It is up to others to comment if they have any new thoughts," Rasmussen told reporters in parliament.

In the early 1990s Denmark had championed Rushdie's fight against the "fatwa" death sentence pronounced on him by Iranian religious leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini for alleged blasphemy against Islam in his book "The Satanic Verses".

Quoting sources in Washington, the Copenhagen daily Politiken on Monday said the CIA had tipped off the Danish government that Iran had "concrete and specific" plans to kill Rushdie in Copenhagen on November 14, when he was due to receive a European Union literary prize.
According to these sources, the Danish government took the CIA warning "very seriously", the newspaper wrote.
Similar reports were published in Monday's Los Angeles Times, which said U.S. government officials confirmed them.
A major political row broke out in November over Rushdie's visit to Copenhagen to receive the European Union's 20,000 Ecu ($24,870) Aristeion Literature Prize.
The government initially banned him on security grounds but changed its mind in the face of domestic and international condemnation and threats of a no-confidence motion in parliament.
Under massive security, Rushdie came to Copenhagen on November 13 to receive the prize along with Austria's Christoph Ransmayr and Danish translator Thorkild Bjoernvig.
The ceremony took place in the Danish capital as Copenhagen is this year's European Cultural Capital.
Rushdie maintained that the British intelligence services had been unaware of any threat to him in Copenhagen.
The original rebuff prompted Rushdie to accuse Copenhagen of "political cowardice", leading to a public apology for the mishandling of the affair from Rasmussen.
